title: Web Accessibility (a11y)
summary: **Accessibility (a11y)** means building pages everyone can use, including people with disabilities. It rests on **WCAG**'s POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust): start with semantic HTML, provide `alt` text, ensure full keyboard navigation and visible focus, meet color-contrast minimums, and respect the **accessibility tree** that screen readers consume.

subtopics.title: WCAG & the POUR principles
subtopics.explanation: The Web Content Accessibility Guidelines organize accessibility into four principles — Perceivable (content can be sensed, e.g. alt text, captions), Operable (everything works by keyboard), Understandable (clear, predictable UI and language), and Robust (works across browsers and assistive tech). Conformance levels are A, AA (the common legal target), and AAA.
subtopics.example: POUR: Perceivable · Operable · Understandable · Robust → target WCAG 2.1 AA

subtopics.title: Semantic HTML first
subtopics.explanation: The first rule of accessibility is to use the right native element. A <button> is focusable, keyboard-operable, and announced as a button for free; a <div onclick> is none of those without extra work. Native semantics populate the accessibility tree correctly, so reach for ARIA only when no element fits.

subtopics.title: Alt text for images
subtopics.explanation: Every needs an alt attribute. Describe the image's purpose concisely for content images; use an empty alt="" for purely decorative images so screen readers skip them. Don't start with 'image of' (the reader already says that), and convey the information the image carries, not its filename.

subtopics.title: Keyboard navigation & focus
subtopics.explanation: Every interactive element must be reachable and usable with the keyboard alone (Tab to move, Enter/Space to activate). Keep a visible focus indicator (never remove outline without a replacement), maintain a logical tab order (follow DOM order; avoid positive tabindex), and manage focus in modals and dynamic content.

subtopics.title: Color contrast
subtopics.explanation: Text must contrast enough with its background to be readable: WCAG AA requires 4.5:1 for normal text and 3:1 for large text and UI components. Never rely on color alone to convey meaning (e.g., red 'error' text also needs an icon or label) since color-blind users may not perceive the difference.
subtopics.example: /* AA needs ≥ 4.5:1 for body text */ color: #1f2937; background: #fff;

subtopics.title: The accessibility tree & screen readers
subtopics.explanation: Browsers build an accessibility tree from the DOM — a model of each element's role, name, state, and value. Screen readers (NVDA, VoiceOver, JAWS) read this tree aloud and let users navigate by landmarks and headings. Semantic HTML and correct labels populate it accurately; div soup leaves it empty and confusing.

subtopics.title: Skip links
subtopics.explanation: A skip link is the first focusable element, hidden until focused, that jumps keyboard and screen-reader users past repetitive navigation straight to <main>. It saves them from tabbing through the same menu on every page and is a quick, high-value accessibility win.

foundations.overview: Accessibility is the practice of building web experiences usable by people with disabilities — visual, motor, auditory, cognitive — and by extension, everyone. Most of it isn't extra work bolted on at the end; it's using HTML correctly: semantic elements, alt text, labels, keyboard support, and sufficient contrast. The standard is WCAG, structured around four POUR principles, and AA conformance is the typical legal and practical target.
foundations.formalDefinition: Web accessibility is the inclusive design and implementation of websites so that people with disabilities can perceive, understand, navigate, and interact with them, as codified by the W3C's Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) under the Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, and Robust principles.
foundations.whyItMatters: Roughly one in six people has a disability; accessibility determines whether they can use your product at all. It's also a legal requirement in many jurisdictions (ADA, Section 508, EAA), overlaps heavily with SEO and good UX, and is a standard topic in front-end interviews and audits.
foundations.mentalModel: Imagine using your site with your eyes closed and only a keyboard, listening to a screen reader narrate it. Can you tell what each control is? Can you reach and operate everything? Can you find the main content quickly? If yes, the page is accessible; the markup is what makes that narration coherent.
foundations.browserPerspective: The browser builds an accessibility tree alongside the DOM, computing each element's role, accessible name, state, and value. Assistive technologies read that tree, not your visual layout. Semantic elements and proper labels feed it correct data; non-semantic markup leaves roles unknown and names blank.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Accessible patterns appear everywhere good teams ship: labeled form inputs, alt text on images, keyboard-operable menus and modals with focus management, skip links, visible focus rings, and AA-contrast color systems baked into design tokens.
foundations.businessImpact: Accessibility broadens the addressable audience, reduces legal and reputational risk (lawsuits over inaccessible sites are common), and improves SEO and overall usability — all of which affect reach and revenue.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Doing it with semantics and the right elements minimizes custom ARIA and JavaScript, making components simpler and more robust. Retrofitting accessibility late is far more expensive than building it in.
foundations.performanceImpact: Accessibility doesn't slow rendering; in fact leaning on native semantics over ARIA-laden div soup keeps markup leaner. The cost is upfront discipline, not runtime performance.
commonUseCases: Semantic landmarks and headings for screen-reader navigation
alt text on images (empty alt for decorative)
Fully keyboard-operable controls with visible focus
AA color contrast and not relying on color alone
Skip-to-content link and focus management in modals

commonMisconceptions.myth: Accessibility is a small niche audience, so it's optional.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Disabilities (including temporary and situational ones like a broken arm or bright sunlight) affect a large share of users, and accessibility is legally required in many places. It's also baseline good UX.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Adding ARIA roles everywhere makes a page accessible.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The first rule of ARIA is don't use ARIA if a native element does the job. Incorrect ARIA often makes things worse; semantic HTML should come first and ARIA only fills gaps.

commonMisconceptions.myth: Passing an automated checker means the page is accessible.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Automated tools catch only ~30–50% of issues (contrast, missing alt, etc.). Keyboard testing and screen-reader testing are needed to confirm real usability.

visualExplorer.title: From DOM to spoken page: the accessibility pipeline
visualExplorer.caption: Trace how your markup becomes what a screen-reader user hears, and where each a11y practice plugs in.

config.intro: Assistive tech never sees your CSS — it reads an accessibility tree the browser computes from your HTML. Here's how the right practices shape it.

steps.name: Write semantic HTML
steps.detail: Use real elements (button, nav, label, h1–h6) so each gets a correct role and behavior without extra code.

steps.name: Provide names & alt text
steps.detail: alt on images and labels on inputs give elements an accessible name the tree exposes.

steps.name: Browser builds the a11y tree
steps.detail: The browser computes role, name, state, and value for each node from the DOM and any ARIA.

steps.name: Ensure keyboard operability
steps.detail: Tab order and visible focus let users reach and activate every control without a mouse.

steps.name: Screen reader narrates
steps.detail: NVDA/VoiceOver read the tree, announcing 'button, Delete' or jumping by landmark and heading.

steps.name: User navigates & acts
steps.detail: Skip links, logical headings, and focus management let the user move efficiently and complete tasks.

interactiveExamples.title: Accessible form vs. unlabeled inputs
interactiveExamples.explanation: Each input is tied to a <label> via for/id, so screen readers announce the field's name and clicking the label focuses the field. Without labels, users hear only 'edit text' with no idea what to type.

files.index.html:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html lang="en">
<body>
  <form>
    <label for="name">Full name</label>
    <input id="name" type="text" autocomplete="name">

    <label for="email">Email</label>
    <input id="email" type="email" autocomplete="email">

    <button type="submit">Sign up</button>
  </form>
</body>
</html>

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A form with labeled name and email fields and a Sign up button; labels are clickable and focus shows a visible ring.

interactiveExamples.title: Skip link + landmarks + alt text
interactiveExamples.explanation: A skip link (hidden until focused) lets keyboard users jump past the nav to <main>. Landmarks and an informative alt round out a screen-reader-friendly page.

interactiveExamples.expectedOutput: A page with a header/nav and main; pressing Tab first reveals a 'Skip to content' link that jumps focus to the main region.

codeLab.title: Make the widget accessible
codeLab.instructions: This 'button' is a clickable div with an icon-only image and no label. Rewrite it as a real <button>, give the image meaningful alt text (or make the button's text the label), and ensure it's keyboard operable.

files.styles.css:
body { font-family: system-ui; padding: 24px; }
.btn { display: inline-flex; padding: 8px; border: 1px solid #ccc; border-radius: 6px; cursor: pointer; }

codeLab.expectedOutput: A real button with an accessible label that works on click and via Enter/Space, with a visible focus ring.
hints: A native <button> is focusable and responds to Enter/Space automatically — no tabindex or key handlers needed.
Give the button visible text ('Save') as its label; mark the decorative icon with alt="" so it isn't announced twice.

debuggingLab.title: Keyboard users get stuck and can't see focus
debuggingLab.symptom: An audit reports that a custom control can't be reached or activated by keyboard, and that there's no visible focus indicator anywhere on the page.

files.index.html: Run A link

debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: Two issues. First, a <span> with onclick is not focusable or keyboard-operable — it can't be reached with Tab and won't respond to Enter/Space, so keyboard and screen-reader users can't use it. Second, the global '*:focus { outline: none }' strips the focus indicator from everything, leaving keyboard users with no idea where they are.
commonMistakes: Using a div/span with onclick instead of a real <button>.
Removing focus outlines globally without providing a visible replacement.
Relying on the mouse and never testing with Tab/Enter.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Use a native button so the control is keyboard-operable, and restore a clear, visible focus indicator.

theory.question: What is web accessibility and what are the WCAG POUR principles?
theory.directAnswer: Web accessibility means designing and building sites so people with disabilities can perceive, operate, understand, and interact with them. The WCAG standard organizes this into four POUR principles: Perceivable (content can be sensed — alt text, captions, contrast), Operable (everything works by keyboard, no traps), Understandable (clear language and predictable behavior), and Robust (works reliably across browsers and assistive tech). AA is the common conformance target.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Inclusive design so disabled users can use the web, formalized by WCAG's POUR principles.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A large share of users have disabilities, and laws require equal access; guidelines give a measurable standard.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Practices map to POUR and to WCAG success criteria at levels A, AA, and AAA.

theory.whyImportant: It's an ethical, legal, and UX requirement and a standard interview/audit topic.
theory.realWorldExample: A screen-reader user navigates by landmarks and hears 'button, Save' because the page used semantic HTML and proper labels.

nestedTopics.title: Conformance levels
nestedTopics.explanation: A, AA, and AAA; AA is the usual legal and practical target.

nestedTopics.title: Beyond automation
nestedTopics.explanation: Automated tools catch only part of issues; keyboard and screen-reader testing are essential.

nestedTopics.title: Overlap with UX/SEO
nestedTopics.explanation: Accessible structure also improves usability and search ranking.

followUps.question: Why is semantic HTML the foundation of accessibility?
followUps.answer: Native elements come with correct roles, names, states, and keyboard behavior, populating the accessibility tree correctly so screen readers work without extra ARIA.

followUps.question: Do automated checkers prove a page is accessible?
followUps.answer: No — they catch roughly a third to half of issues like contrast and missing alt; you still need manual keyboard and screen-reader testing.

theory.question: What is the accessibility tree and how do screen readers use it?
theory.directAnswer: The accessibility tree is a parallel structure the browser builds from the DOM, computing each element's role (button, link, heading), accessible name (its label/alt/text), state (checked, expanded), and value. Screen readers like NVDA, VoiceOver, and JAWS read this tree — not your visual CSS — to announce elements and let users navigate by landmarks and headings. Semantic HTML and correct labels populate it accurately.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: The browser's semantic model of the page that assistive tech consumes.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Assistive tech needs a structured, role-aware representation rather than pixels.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The browser derives role/name/state/value from elements, attributes, and ARIA, exposing it via platform accessibility APIs.

theory.whyImportant: It's the bridge between your markup and the screen-reader experience; understanding it explains why semantics matter.
theory.realWorldExample: A <nav> becomes role 'navigation' and a <button>Save</button> becomes 'button, Save' — both navigable without any ARIA.

nestedTopics.title: Accessible name
nestedTopics.explanation: Computed from text content, alt, aria-label, or associated <label>.

nestedTopics.title: Role and state
nestedTopics.explanation: Roles describe what a thing is; states (expanded, checked) describe its condition.

nestedTopics.title: ARIA overrides
nestedTopics.explanation: ARIA attributes can change an element's role/name/state in the tree — powerful, but easy to get wrong, so prefer native semantics.

followUps.question: How can you inspect the accessibility tree?
followUps.answer: Chrome and Firefox DevTools have an Accessibility panel showing each node's computed role, name, and state, which is invaluable for debugging.

followUps.question: What happens if an element has no accessible name?
followUps.answer: A control like a button with no text, label, or aria-label is announced only by its role (e.g., 'button'), leaving the user no idea what it does — always ensure an accessible name.

scenario.question: An accessibility audit on your checkout flow flags: images with no alt, form inputs with no labels, a modal that doesn't trap focus, and low-contrast 'error' text shown only in red. How do you remediate?
scenario.directAnswer: Add meaningful alt to content images (alt="" for decorative ones); associate every input with a <label> via for/id so it gets an accessible name; in the modal, move focus into it on open, trap Tab within it, return focus to the trigger on close, and support Escape; and fix the errors to meet 4.5:1 contrast while adding a text label or icon so meaning isn't conveyed by color alone.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Remediation across the four most common audit categories: images, forms, focus, and contrast.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Each gap blocks a specific group — blind users, screen-reader users, keyboard users, color-blind users.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Labels and alt feed the accessibility tree; focus management keeps keyboard users oriented; contrast and non-color cues ensure perceivability.

scenario.whyImportant: Checkout is revenue-critical; these are the most frequent and impactful audit failures.

nestedTopics.title: Focus trapping
nestedTopics.explanation: Keep Tab within a modal and restore focus to the trigger on close.

nestedTopics.title: Don't rely on color
nestedTopics.explanation: Pair color with text/icon so color-blind users perceive state.

followUps.question: How would you verify the fixes?
followUps.answer: Run axe/Lighthouse for automated checks, tab through the flow checking focus order and visibility, and complete a purchase using only a screen reader.

coding.question: Write an accessible page skeleton: a skip link, semantic landmarks, a labeled search form, an image with alt, and a real button — all keyboard operable.
coding.thoughtProcess: Lead with a skip link as the first focusable element so keyboard users can bypass nav. Use header/nav/main/footer landmarks. Label the search input with a <label> tied via for/id. Give the image meaningful alt. Use a native <button type=submit>. Rely on native semantics so everything is keyboard operable without extra ARIA.

coding.lineByLine: The skip link is the first focusable element so keyboard users can jump straight to #main. header/nav/main/footer create landmarks the screen reader can navigate, and nav gets an aria-label to distinguish it. The search form labels its input via for/id so the field has an accessible name, and uses a native submit <button> that's keyboard operable for free. The image carries descriptive alt. No custom ARIA is needed because the native elements supply correct roles.

alternativeApproaches.title: Visually-hidden label
alternativeApproaches.explanation: If the design has no room for a visible label, use a visually-hidden label or aria-label instead of dropping the label entirely — the field still needs an accessible name.

followUps.question: Why associate a label with for/id instead of just placing text nearby?
followUps.answer: The for/id association gives the input a programmatic accessible name and makes the label clickable to focus the field; nearby text alone isn't linked to the control in the accessibility tree.

followUps.question: When is aria-label appropriate instead of a visible label?
followUps.answer: Use aria-label (or a visually-hidden label) when the design genuinely can't show visible text, such as an icon-only button — the control still needs an accessible name, just not a visible one.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Bake accessibility into the design system: components render semantic elements, enforce labels (a button without an accessible name fails a lint/test), expose focus styles, and use AA-contrast tokens — so every team inherits accessible primitives by default.
productionDeepDive.performance: Accessibility doesn't add runtime cost; favoring native semantics over heavy ARIA-and-JS reimplementations keeps components lighter and the accessibility tree accurate without extra work.
productionDeepDive.security: Not a security boundary per se, but ensure dynamically injected content keeps labels and roles intact and that error/status messages are announced (aria-live) without leaking sensitive data.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Across large products, automate checks (axe in unit/e2e tests, Lighthouse/pa11y in CI), gate merges on accessibility lint rules, and maintain documented accessible patterns for menus, modals, and tabs so quality scales with the codebase.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Semantic, well-labeled markup is self-documenting and easier to evolve than custom ARIA widgets; centralizing patterns prevents each team from reinventing inaccessible components.
productionDeepDive.observability: Combine automated CI checks with periodic manual audits — keyboard-only walkthroughs and screen-reader testing of key flows — plus user feedback channels, since tooling catches only part of real-world issues.

caseStudies.problem: Legal requirements (ADA, Section 508, EAA) and audits exposing keyboard and labeling failures.
caseStudies.solution: Accessible design system, semantic-first components, CI a11y gates, and manual screen-reader QA on critical flows.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Upfront investment and discipline vs. far lower remediation cost and legal exposure.
caseStudies.lessons: Building accessibility in from the start is dramatically cheaper than retrofitting it after a lawsuit or audit.

projectBuilder.summary: Make your portfolio accessible end to end: skip link, semantic landmarks, alt text, labeled contact form, keyboard-operable controls with visible focus, and AA contrast.
requirements: A skip-to-content link as the first focusable element
Semantic landmarks (header/nav/main/footer) and a logical heading outline
Meaningful alt text on images (empty alt for decorative)
A contact form with labels and a real submit button
Visible focus styles and AA color contrast throughout
projectBuilder.architecture: A semantic single page where every interactive element is native and keyboard-operable, content images have alt, and a skip link plus landmarks let assistive-tech users navigate efficiently.

steps.title: Skip link & landmarks
steps.instructions: Add a skip-to-content link and wrap regions in header/nav/main/footer.
steps.checkpoint: Tabbing first reveals the skip link, which jumps focus to main.

steps.title: Images & form
steps.instructions: Add alt to images and labels (for/id) to all form fields with a native submit button.
steps.checkpoint: A screen reader announces each field's name and each image's purpose.

steps.title: Focus & contrast
steps.instructions: Add visible :focus-visible styles and verify text meets 4.5:1 contrast.
steps.checkpoint: axe/Lighthouse report no critical accessibility violations.

enhancements: Add a visually-hidden helper class for off-screen labels
Add aria-live status messaging to the contact form
Test the whole page with VoiceOver/NVDA

keyTakeaways: Accessibility (a11y) means building for everyone, including people with disabilities; WCAG's POUR principles (Perceivable, Operable, Understandable, Robust) are the standard, with AA the common target.
Semantic HTML first: native elements supply correct roles, names, and keyboard behavior — use ARIA only when no element fits.
Provide alt text (empty for decorative images), full keyboard operability with a visible focus indicator, and AA color contrast without relying on color alone.
Screen readers read the browser's accessibility tree (role/name/state/value), not your CSS — correct markup and labels populate it accurately.
Skip links and landmarks speed navigation; automated checkers catch only part of issues, so keyboard and screen-reader testing are essential.
